passage: Suppose you and a colleague whom you regard as your equal in competence and care examine the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions. Neither of you has information the other lacks; neither has reason to think the other was tired or distracted. What should you do? An influential answer holds that you should move towards your colleague's view, giving her opinion the same weight as your own. The thought behind it is simple. From a neutral standpoint, the disagreement is evidence that one of you has erred, and you have no reason, independent of the dispute itself, to think the error is hers rather than yours. To stand firm would be to treat the mere fact that a conclusion is yours as a reason to favour it.

This principle seems to me correct over a wide range of cases, and it is more demanding than most people find comfortable. It condemns the familiar move of discounting a dissenter precisely because she dissents: 'she is usually so sensible, but on this question she has plainly lost her way'. If the only evidence that she has lost her way is that she disagrees with you, the reasoning simply assumes what is in question.

Yet the principle cannot be applied without qualification. Imagine two equally able auditors reviewing the same short ledger, one of whom concludes that the accounts balance while the other reports that the firm's assets exceed the number of grains of sand on the earth. The first auditor need not split the difference. Her confidence that her colleague has blundered does not rest on her own conclusion about the ledger; it rests on the absurdity of his, which she can recognise without relying on the reasoning they disagree about. What licenses holding firm, then, is not that a view is one's own but that one has grounds, independent of the dispute, for locating the error on the other side. The equal-weight principle survives, but it turns out to be a claim about what to do when such independent grounds are absent, not a rule that applies whatever one knows.

Critics sometimes press a further objection: since thoughtful people disagree about the equal-weight principle itself, the principle seems to require its own defenders to lose confidence in it. This is less damaging than it first appears. A principle about how to respond to disagreement may well recommend reduced confidence in itself without thereby becoming false; it would show only that the matter is genuinely hard, which no one denied. What the objection does reveal is that conciliation cannot be the whole story about rational belief. A thinker who revised every view the moment a peer dissented would soon have no settled views left to revise, and some account is still owed of what entitles anyone to a starting point.

passage: Intellectual humility is praised more often than it is defined, and the praise tends to blur it with other things. Sometimes it is equated with low confidence, as if the humble thinker were one who held every opinion loosely. Sometimes it is identified with deference, the willingness to yield to those who know more. And sometimes it means no more than a modest manner, the habit of prefacing one's claims with 'I may be wrong, but'. Each of these captures something, yet none of them can be the virtue itself, because each can be present where humility is absent and absent where humility is present.

Take low confidence first. A person may be unsure of everything out of sheer timidity, believing too little rather than too much, and timidity of this kind is no more admirable than arrogance; it is merely a different way of misjudging one's evidence. Conversely, someone may be entirely certain that the earth orbits the sun, and rightly so, without any failure of humility. Deference fares no better. It is often wise, but a thinker who deferred to every apparent authority would be credulous rather than humble, and one who refused to defer to a genuine expert on a question outside her competence might be guilty of several faults without its being clear that humility is the one she lacks. As for the modest manner, it concerns how one presents oneself to others, and it can coexist with a private conviction that one is never mistaken. The phrase 'I may be wrong' is cheap to say.

A more promising account locates humility in a person's relation to her own limitations. The humble thinker is one who notices the gaps in her knowledge, the places where her reasoning is shaky and the biases to which she is prone, and who takes these into account: she seeks out the evidence she lacks, rechecks the steps she is unsure of, and discounts the conclusions she has special reason to want. This is compatible with great confidence where her grounds are good. Indeed, it is partly because she is alert to where her grounds are poor that her confidence elsewhere deserves to be taken seriously. Her humility, on this view, is not a feeling about herself but a settled pattern of attention and correction, visible chiefly in what she does whenever her own judgement is at stake.

It may be objected that this account makes humility indistinguishable from good reasoning in general. Anyone who reasons well, after all, attends to the strength of her evidence. But the two can come apart. A scientist may be superb at weighing evidence about the world and yet curiously blind to the ways in which her own ambitions shape which questions she asks and which results she finds convincing. Her failure is not a failure to reason about stars or cells; it is a failure to treat herself as one more possible source of error. That reflexive attention, directed at the reasoner rather than at the subject matter, is what the word humility usefully picks out.

The account has a further merit: it explains why humility can be overdone. A person preoccupied with her own limitations, forever cataloguing the ways in which she might be mistaken, may become unable to act on what she knows or to contribute what she has to offer. Owning one's limitations includes keeping them in proportion, and the thinker who is paralysed by self-scrutiny has misjudged them as surely as the one who ignores them.

passage: Of all the performing arts, dance has the most fragile relation to its own past. A play survives in its script and a symphony in its score, so that later generations, whatever they make of these documents, at least have something to argue over. A dance, by contrast, has for most of its history existed only while it was being danced and in the memories of those who danced it. It is tempting to conclude that dance is therefore an art without a history, or one whose history is a long series of losses, and that the remedy is simply better documentation.

There have been serious attempts at such documentation. Systems of dance notation have been devised that record the position of each part of the body over time, and film and video now capture performances that would once have vanished. These tools are valuable, but they have not displaced the older method of transmission, in which a dancer who has performed a role teaches it directly to a younger dancer, in a studio, by demonstration and correction. Many companies that hold detailed records of their repertoire still rely on such teaching when a work is revived, and they tend to treat the written record as an aid to memory rather than as the work itself.

The reason is not mere conservatism. What passes from one body to another in the studio includes things that a notation or a recording captures poorly or not at all: the weight of a movement, the quality of attention behind it, the reasons a gesture is timed as it is. A film shows what a particular dancer did on a particular night, including her idiosyncrasies and her mistakes; it cannot say which of those features belong to the choreography and which belong to her. A teacher who has danced the role can make that distinction, or at least has a considered view about it, and passes the view on along with the steps.

This method has an obvious cost. Each transmission is also an interpretation, and over several generations a dance may drift a long way from what its maker first set. Yet the drift is not simply a corruption. A dance kept alive in bodies is continually tested against the dancers who perform it, and the features that survive are usually those that dancers have found to matter. The archive of dance, on this view, is not mainly a shelf of documents but a lineage of people, and its gaps are the price of its being alive.

passage: A familiar way of thinking about pollution treats it as a simple wrong: one party harms another, and the law should stop the harm or make the harmer pay. An influential argument in economics asks us to look at the situation differently. Suppose the smoke from a small factory soils the washing of a few households nearby. The harm, on this view, is reciprocal: to protect the washing is to restrict the factory, and to protect the factory is to burden the households. If the parties could bargain freely and cheaply, the argument runs, they would arrive at the efficient outcome whoever held the legal right. If the households had the right to clean air, the factory would pay them to tolerate some smoke whenever its gains exceeded their losses; if the factory had the right to emit, the households would pay it to fit a filter whenever the filter cost less than the damage it prevented.

The conclusion is often summarised as a reason for governments to stand aside: define property rights clearly, and private bargaining will do the rest. That reading takes the conditional for the claim. The striking result holds only when bargaining is nearly costless, and the more interesting lesson lies in how rarely that condition is met. A few households and one factory can meet around a table. A city of several million people breathing the exhaust of a million vehicles cannot. Each resident's share of the harm is small, working out who caused how much of it is difficult, and every resident has a reason to let others negotiate and pay while enjoying the cleaner air for nothing. The costs of finding the parties, measuring the damage and enforcing an agreement swamp whatever gains the bargain might bring.

Read in this way, the argument is less a case against regulation than a map of where it is needed. Where the parties are few, the harm is visible and agreements can be checked, private settlement may indeed work better than a rule imposed from outside; the neighbours of a noisy workshop may settle a dispute over evening hours more sensibly than any ordinance could. Where the parties are many and scattered, the same reasoning that praises bargaining in principle explains why it will not happen in practice, and why a tax, a standard or a tradable permit can stand in for a negotiation that no one is able to hold.

None of this makes the assignment of rights a matter of indifference. Even when bargaining would reach the same physical outcome, it matters a great deal who pays whom. A rule that gives the factory the right to pollute leaves the households poorer by the price of their clean air; a rule that gives them the right leaves the factory's owners poorer instead. Efficiency may be blind to that difference. Those who live downwind are not.

passage: It is easy to write the history of urban smell as a simple story of progress. Pre-modern cities stank of sewage, tanneries, slaughterhouses and unwashed bodies; reformers built drains and water supplies; the stench retreated. Every part of this is true, and anyone inclined to romanticise the crowded streets of earlier centuries should be reminded of it. But the story assumes that the nose is a constant instrument, registering the same smells with the same disgust in every age, and that assumption does not survive a reading of the sources.

Residents of older towns certainly complained about smells, but their complaints were selective. Odours that later generations would find unbearable, such as the smell of a dung heap beside a house, were often accepted as part of ordinary life, while others, associated with particular trades or with neighbours who were disliked, drew sustained protest. What made a smell intolerable depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean. And from the late eighteenth century onwards, in much of Europe, smells came to mean something very specific. Under the theory that disease spread through foul air, a bad smell was not merely unpleasant; it was a warning, perhaps even the danger itself.

The theory was wrong, but it was productive. Because it identified smell with sickness, it gave reformers a reason, and a sense of urgency, to remove the sources of smell, and many of the measures they took, from covered sewers to the regular removal of refuse, did reduce disease, though for reasons they did not understand. A mistaken idea about how illness spread thus helped to justify works whose real benefit lay elsewhere. When the germ theory displaced it, smell lost its medical authority; it did not lose its power.

Freed from medicine, the vocabulary of smell attached itself more firmly to persons. Middle-class households that had learned to fear foul air now learned to fear the odour of the poor, the newcomer and the manual worker, and the judgement passed easily from bodies to character. The cleaner cities became, the more a lingering smell could serve as a mark of social distance. This is why a history of smell cannot be only a history of drains; it must also be a history of who was allowed to call whom offensive, and of how a sense that seems the most immediate of all has always been schooled.

passage: A respectable argument holds that negative criticism of new books is a waste of everyone's time. So many books are published each year that no critic can notice more than a sliver of them; the space a journal devotes to criticism is therefore precious, and to spend it explaining why a book is bad is to deny it to a book that deserves attention. On this view the most damning verdict a critic can deliver is silence. A poor book left unmentioned simply sinks, and nothing is lost except the pleasure that some critics take in wounding. The position has the further appeal of seeming kind, which is no small recommendation in a literary world where writers and critics are often the same people.

The argument is tidy, but it quietly assumes that the only job of criticism is to guide readers in choosing what to read. If that were so, the notice of a weak book would indeed be wasted, since a reader who is told merely to skip something has learned nothing that he could use elsewhere. But criticism has always done something besides sorting. A careful account of why a book fails is also an account of what success would have looked like, and in giving it the critic makes public a set of standards that readers can test, dispute and apply for themselves. The reader who follows a well-argued case against a novel he admired may end unconvinced, yet he will read the next novel more alertly.

There is a further cost to silence. If critics write only about the books they admire, praise becomes the sole currency of criticism, and like any currency issued without limit it loses its value. A notice that can only ever say yes tells the reader very little, because its enthusiasm is not the outcome of a judgement that could have gone the other way. Readers soon learn to discount it, as they discount the admiring phrases printed on the cover of every new book, and the critic whose praise is sincere is then heard no more clearly than the publicist. The possibility of dispraise is what gives praise its meaning.

None of this licenses cruelty, and the case for restraint does have force in one kind of instance. A modest first novel from a small press, which few people will encounter anyway, gains nothing from a public demolition, and neither do its readers. The negative notice earns its space when the book in question is prominent: widely praised, heavily promoted, or likely to shape what others write. There the critic who dissents is not kicking someone who is down but contesting a reputation that is already shaping public taste, and that is among the most useful things criticism can do.

passage: It has become a commonplace that rewarding people for doing what they already enjoy can make them enjoy it less. Picture a child who draws for the pleasure of it and is then promised a prize for each picture. While the prizes continue, the drawing may increase. When they stop, the child may draw less than before the prizes began, as though the activity had been converted from play into work and then left unpaid. The phenomenon is real, and it has been reproduced often enough to deserve to be taken seriously. What is less often noticed is how many conditions it depends upon, and how quickly it fades when they are absent.

The effect appears most reliably when the reward is tangible, expected in advance and given for doing the task rather than for doing it well. A prize announced beforehand and handed over for every picture invites the child to understand the drawing as a means to the prize. An unexpected treat, by contrast, cannot have been the reason for drawing, and praise that tells the child something about the quality of the work may even strengthen interest, since it feeds the sense of competence that made the activity enjoyable in the first place. The same physical reward can therefore have opposite effects depending on what it communicates to the person who receives it.

Equally important, the effect presupposes that there was interest to undermine. Many tasks that people are paid or rewarded for, from sorting files to practising scales, hold little intrinsic appeal at the outset, and for these, rewards cannot crowd out an enjoyment that was never there. Indeed, a reward may keep someone at a dull task long enough for skill to grow and for the task itself to become absorbing, so that interest arrives because of the incentive rather than in spite of it.

The sensible conclusion lies between two slogans. Those who say that rewards destroy motivation generalise from a narrow set of conditions; those who say that people simply do whatever they are paid to do ignore the conditions entirely. The better question in any particular case is how the reward is likely to be read: as an attempt to control behaviour that would otherwise not occur, or as information about how well something is being done. The first reading tends to erode interest in activities that people already value; the second tends to support it.

passage: Modern moral intuition tends to reserve its highest praise for the gift that expects nothing in return. A present given with an eye to what will come back seems to us slightly tarnished, closer to a trade dressed up in ribbon than to generosity. Anthropologists who have studied exchange in a wide range of societies have long found this intuition puzzling, not because people elsewhere are more calculating, but because in most places the obligation to return is understood as part of what a gift is. To receive is to accept a tie; to fail to reciprocate is not merely rude but a refusal of the relationship the gift proposed.

Consider how carefully the timing and size of a return are managed in many communities. A neighbour who sends back a dish of sweets on the very evening she received one has not discharged a debt so much as declined a friendship; the speed of her reply announces that she wants the account closed. A return that matches the original exactly carries a similar message. What sustains the bond is a return that comes later and differs slightly in value, so that one party is always, for the moment, a little in the other's debt. On this view the imbalance is not a flaw to be corrected but the mechanism by which the relationship is kept running: an account that is never quite settled is an account that remains open.

Seen in this light, the free gift is less an ideal than an anomaly. A gift that truly demanded nothing would create no tie, and a society composed only of such gifts would be a collection of strangers who happened to hand each other things. It is telling that the gifts we most often describe as free, such as anonymous donations, are precisely those designed to prevent any relationship between giver and receiver from forming.

None of this means that the obligation to return is always benign. Where one party can give far more than the other could ever repay, the gift becomes an instrument of domination: the receiver is bound by a debt that cannot be cleared, and gratitude hardens into dependence. Patrons have long understood this, and so have recipients of charity, who sometimes refuse help precisely because they cannot answer it. The lesson, however, is not that we should aspire to gifts without strings. It is that the strings must be ones the receiver is able to hold. A generous act, properly understood, is calibrated to the other person's capacity to reply.

passage: A great deal of advertising tells the viewer almost nothing. A television spot in which a famous athlete drinks a soft drink on a beach conveys no fact about the drink's price, ingredients or taste that a sceptical viewer could check, and critics of advertising have long drawn what seems the obvious conclusion: if the message carries no information, the money spent on it is either wasted or devoted to manipulation, persuading people to want things by associating them with glamour. The conclusion is natural, but it rests on the assumption that whatever an advertisement communicates must be contained in what it says or shows, and that assumption is open to question.

Consider the matter from the firm's side. A company launching a product that is cheap to try, such as a breakfast cereal or a shampoo, makes its money not from the first purchase but from the repeat purchases of customers who liked it. A firm confident that its product is good therefore expects a long stream of returns from anyone it persuades to try it once, whereas a firm that knows its product is mediocre expects most of those who try it never to return. Lavish advertising is accordingly worth far more to the first firm than to the second, and a consumer who sees a product advertised extravagantly may reasonably infer that its maker is wagering on repeat business. On this view the expense of the advertisement is itself the message, and the athlete and the beach matter chiefly because everyone can see that they cost a fortune.

The argument has real force, but its reach is limited. It applies most clearly to what economists call experience goods, whose quality can be judged only after use, and only where repeat purchase is likely; a firm selling something that people buy once in a lifetime gains little from the signal, because satisfied customers will not return in any case. For goods whose qualities can be inspected before purchase, such as the dimensions of a table or the fare for a train journey, advertising informs directly and requires no signalling story at all. Nor does the argument show that every extravagant campaign is a reliable signal, since a firm may overspend from vanity or miscalculation, and imitators may learn to mimic the outward appearance of expense more cheaply than it seems.

A familiar objection is that ordinary consumers do not reason in this way, since nobody watching a soft drink advertisement contemplates the economics of repeat purchase. The objection misunderstands what the argument requires. Consumers need not reconstruct the logic; it is enough that they follow a rule of thumb, such as trusting brands they have heard of, and that the rule tends, on the whole, to reward them. The signalling account does not vindicate advertising, and it leaves the question of manipulation entirely open. What it does establish is that an advertisement without content is not, for that reason alone, an advertisement without meaning.

passage: Public life has an elaborate culture of speaking and almost none of listening. Schools hold debating contests, organisations train their staff in presentation, and the history of rhetoric is largely a history of techniques for the person holding the floor. Listening, by contrast, is treated as what happens automatically when someone else is talking, a passive condition rather than an activity. Nobody is coached in it, and nobody wins a prize for it.

This neglect would matter less if listening were in fact passive. It is not. To follow an argument one disagrees with, a person has to hold its parts in mind long enough to see how they connect, resist the urge to compose a reply while the speaker is still in the middle of a sentence, and notice the difference between what was said and what one expected to hear. Each of these is effortful, and each can be done well or badly. Anyone who has watched a meeting in which three people answer a point that nobody made has seen what happens when it is done badly.

One objection is that a culture of listening would favour the patient over the right. If every view must be heard out in full, the argument runs, then bad ideas gain a hearing they have not earned, and those who are merely persistent will exhaust everyone else. There is something to this. Listening is not the same as agreeing, and a meeting that cannot end because everyone must be fully heard is not a model of deliberation. But the objection mistakes the purpose. Careful listening is valuable less because it is fair to the speaker than because it is useful to the listener: a person who has understood an opposing view can answer the strongest form of it, and can sometimes discover that the disagreement was smaller than it looked.

Nor is it obvious that listening must be slow. Much of the time lost in public argument is lost to misunderstanding, to replies aimed at positions no one holds and to corrections of those replies. A discussion in which each participant first restated the other's point before answering it might take longer at each step and less time overall. If that is so, the case for teaching listening is not a plea for patience but a practical one, and it is odd that institutions so devoted to efficient communication have left half of communication untaught.

passage: A parable that became famous in the second half of the twentieth century asks us to imagine a pasture open to all. Each herder, reasoning that the benefit of an extra animal is his alone while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, adds another, and then another, until the grass is gone and all are ruined. The moral usually drawn is stark: resources held in common will be destroyed unless they are divided into private plots or placed under the control of the state.

The parable is persuasive, but it describes something that most actual commons are not. In many villages, pastures, woodlots, fishing ponds and irrigation channels have been shared for generations without being exhausted, and not because the villagers were unusually selfless. They were governed by rules. A household might be allowed to graze only as many animals as it could feed through the winter from its own fields; grazing might move between sections of the hill in a fixed rotation; a watchman, paid in grain, might patrol the boundary, and offenders might face fines that rose with each repeated offence. The herders of the parable have no such rules, no means of watching one another and no way of punishing those who cheat. What the parable describes is not a commons but open access, a resource that belongs to no community at all.

This does not mean that village commons always survive. They tend to fail in recognisable circumstances: when outsiders who are not bound by local rules can enter freely, when a distant authority overrides local arrangements with regulations that villagers neither understand nor respect, when migration thins the community so much that no one is left to keep watch, or when a sudden rise in the value of the resource makes cheating more tempting than it has ever been. These are real dangers. But they are dangers to particular institutions, not proof that shared ownership is doomed by human nature.

The practical lesson is that the familiar choice between private property and state control is too narrow. To say so is not to romanticise village life; such arrangements can be strict, and some are unequal, giving larger shares to households that hold more land. Even so, a third possibility, communities managing their own resources by rules they have made and can enforce, has a long record of success, and policy that ignores it may destroy working arrangements in the name of preventing a tragedy that was never going to happen.

passage: When a dominant company is overtaken by a newcomer, the explanation usually offered is some version of complacency: its managers, the story goes, grew comfortable, stopped listening to the market and failed to perceive what was approaching. The story has the appeal of a fable, and it permits the rest of us to believe that an identical fate could be avoided simply by remaining vigilant. Its difficulty is that, in many of the best known cases, the incumbent's managers were neither lazy nor blind. They were doing, carefully and well, exactly what they had been trained to do.

The pattern runs roughly as follows. A new technology appears that is, at first, worse than the existing one by the measures that the incumbent's best customers care about. It is slower, or less precise, or less durable, but it is cheaper and simpler, and it finds a small market among buyers who were never well served by the established product. The incumbent asks its customers whether they want the new thing, and they say no. It examines the margins, and they are thin. It looks at the size of the market, and it is too small to move a company of its scale. Every one of these judgements is correct, and together they lead the firm to put its money where its profits are. Meanwhile the new technology improves, year by year, until it is good enough for the mainstream, and the incumbent discovers that its careful attention to its best customers has left it with nothing to offer the rest.

It may be objected that this account is written with the convenient clarity of hindsight, since for every cheap technology that grew up to displace its betters, many others remained toys and disappeared, and an incumbent that chased all of them would have squandered its resources. The objection is fair, but it strengthens rather than weakens the point. If good managers cannot tell in advance which small markets will matter, then vigilance alone cannot be the remedy, because the problem is not a failure to look but a set of rules for deciding what is worth looking at.

What seems to help is therefore structural rather than psychological: firms that have survived such transitions have often placed the new venture in a separate unit, with its own costs and its own measures of success, small enough that a small market can still excite it. This is no guarantee, since separate units can be starved or smothered by the parent organisation, but the arrangement at least removes the new business from the scrutiny of the rules that would have judged it, correctly by their own lights, not worth the trouble.

passage: It has become common for conservation projects and agricultural agencies to announce that they have 'validated' some piece of local knowledge. Fishers' accounts of where a species gathers to spawn are checked against tagging data; herders' claims about which plants their animals avoid in a dry year are tested in feeding trials; farmers' weather signs are compared with rainfall records. When the local claim survives, it is welcomed into the scientific literature, and the project is praised for taking seriously people whose expertise was long ignored. This is an improvement on simple dismissal. Yet the language of validation carries assumptions that deserve more scrutiny than they usually receive.

The first is that local knowledge is a set of separate statements, each of which can be lifted out and checked on its own. Much of what farmers and fishers know does not take this form. A farmer who decides when to sow may attend at once to the flowering of a particular tree, the behaviour of ants, the smell of the soil and the memory of the last three seasons, weighing them against one another in ways she could not easily put into words. Test any one of these signs in isolation and it may predict rainfall poorly; to conclude that the farmer's knowledge has failed would be to mistake a judgement for a list of rules. What is being evaluated is not what she knows but a fragment translated into a form the evaluator can handle.

The second assumption is that the direction of authority runs one way. Science sets the standard, local knowledge applies for admission, and once admitted it belongs to the literature rather than to the people who held it. Communities have sometimes found that knowledge about medicinal plants or fishing grounds, once published, was used by outsiders in ways they had no say in. Validation, in other words, can be a means of transfer as much as of recognition.

It would be wrong to conclude that local knowledge should be shielded from testing altogether. Some local beliefs are mistaken, as some scientific ones are, and the communities that hold them revise them in the light of experience more often than romantic accounts allow. The objection is not to checking but to a procedure in which only one side checks. Where farmers help decide which questions are asked and how the results will be used, and where scientific claims are also tested against their observations, the two bodies of knowledge can correct each other. That is a more demanding arrangement than validation, and a more honest one.

passage: The phrase 'conspicuous consumption', coined by Thorstein Veblen in the 1890s, named a habit of the wealthy of his day: the purchase of goods whose chief use was to show that one could afford them. The mansion, the carriage and the idle household were, on this account, less comforts than advertisements. The idea proved so useful that it outlived the society that prompted it, and it still shapes how we picture status spending: the logo on the handbag, the oversized car, the watch that costs more than a year's rent.

The picture now misleads more than it reveals, at least at the top. As mass production and global supply chains have made once-rare goods cheap, the handbag and the car have become available, in passable imitations, to almost anyone with a credit card. Display of this kind has lost much of its power to separate, and many of the most advantaged households have turned away from it. Their spending flows instead into things that are hard to see and harder to copy: private tuition and a house in the right school catchment, retirement savings, organic groceries, exercise classes, domestic help that frees time for reading, and clothing whose quality is recognised only by those who know what to look for. The signal, where there is one, is addressed to a narrow audience of peers rather than to the street. Call this inconspicuous consumption.

It would be easy to treat the change as an improvement in taste, a retreat from vulgar display into quieter and more sensible habits. In part it is. Much of this spending yields real benefits in health, in learning and in security, and few would wish the rich to return to buying gold-plated taps. But the shift has two consequences that the language of good taste conceals. The first is that inconspicuous goods are more effective at reproducing advantage than conspicuous ones ever were. A diamond can be sold; a childhood spent in good schools, with books at home and parents who have time, becomes part of a person and can neither be taken away nor easily acquired later. Spending of this kind does not merely display a position; it passes it on.

The second consequence is moral. Conspicuous consumption invited criticism precisely because it was conspicuous. The flashy car was an obvious target for the satirist and the moralist, and its owner could be accused of vanity. Inconspicuous consumption is much harder to criticise, because it presents itself not as display but as virtue: one is not showing off, one is merely eating well, looking after one's health and investing in one's children. The vocabulary that surrounds it, of wellness, sensible choices and doing the best for one's family, offers the satirist nothing obviously vulgar to mock. Those who cannot afford to do the same are not envied so much as quietly judged, as though their diets and their children's results were failures of character rather than of income.

None of this is an accusation of bad faith. It does not require us to think the affluent hypocritical, or the parent paying for tuition secretly bent on buying status; most such choices are made sincerely, for the reasons people give. The point is structural rather than personal. A society in which advantage is transmitted through the visible accumulation of objects at least makes its inequalities legible. One in which advantage flows through habits, schooling and time has made them harder to see, and inequalities that are hard to see are also harder to argue about.

passage: Almost every modern constitution makes room for its own partial suspension. In a war, an epidemic or a sudden collapse of public order, the executive may be permitted to rule by decree, restrict movement or detain people without the usual procedures, on the understanding that these powers serve to preserve the constitutional order rather than to replace it. The logic is respectable. A constitution that made no provision for emergencies would not prevent governments from acting in a crisis; it would simply ensure that they acted outside the law, improvising powers with no defined limits and no defined end.

The danger that emergency provisions are usually designed to guard against is the dramatic one: a leader who declares a crisis in order to abolish the constitution altogether. That danger is real but comparatively rare. The more common pattern is quieter. An emergency is declared for a genuine reason, and then renewed, and renewed again, because the threat has not entirely disappeared and no official wants to be blamed if it returns. Measures adopted as exceptions are gradually written into ordinary statutes, where they no longer need renewal at all. And each emergency lowers the threshold for the next, since officials and citizens alike grow accustomed to powers that once seemed extraordinary.

The standard remedy is the sunset clause, which makes emergency powers lapse after a fixed period unless they are renewed. Sunset clauses are better than nothing, but they tend to turn renewal into a formality, a vote taken under the shadow of the original fear by legislators who see little to gain from being the ones who let the powers lapse. What matters is not whether powers expire but how hard it is to extend them. A more demanding design would require larger majorities for each successive renewal, so that a measure which commanded a bare majority at the outset needed broad agreement to survive a year later, and it would oblige the government to state publicly, each time, why ordinary law is still inadequate to the threat.

Such designs would not prevent a determined government from abusing emergency powers, and no constitutional text can do that alone; courts, a free press and an opposition willing to make itself unpopular all have parts to play. The purpose of the design is more modest: to make normalisation visible and expensive, so that an exception which has outlasted its reasons must be defended openly as a permanent change rather than slipping into permanence unnoticed. A government that genuinely needs lasting powers can still obtain them, but only by persuading a broad majority that the change should be lasting. The test of an emergency regime is less whether it can survive a coup than whether it can end.

passage: It is often said that a tolerant society is one in which people do not mind how others live, but this gets the idea almost exactly backwards. To tolerate something is to put up with it, and one can only put up with what one dislikes or disapproves of. A person who is untroubled by her neighbour's choice of diet, dress or companions is not tolerating that choice; she is simply indifferent to it, and indifference requires no effort and earns no praise. Toleration begins where objection begins: it is the decision not to act against something that one continues to regard as mistaken.

Put this way, toleration can look puzzling, even paradoxical. If I believe that a practice is wrong, how can it be a virtue for me to let it continue? Surely the better person would either stop objecting or start resisting. The puzzle dissolves, however, once we recognise that the tolerant person holds reasons at two distinct levels. At the first level she objects to the practice; at the second level she has reasons, which she judges to be weightier, for not interfering with it: that adults have authority over their own lives, that her own judgement might be wrong, that a society in which everyone enforced their disapproval on everyone else would be unbearable. Consider a mother who thinks her grown son's choice of career foolish and tells him so, but would never dream of threatening to cut him out of her will to force him back. She has not abandoned her objection. She has ranked it beneath something she values more.

Toleration so understood has limits, and they follow from the same structure. Where the second-level reasons give out, as when a practice inflicts harm on people who have not agreed to bear it, the case for restraint weakens and may disappear. A tolerant society is not one that permits everything.

Some critics find the whole idea condescending: to be tolerated, they point out, is to be told that one is disapproved of and merely endured, and they propose that a just society should aim higher, at the positive recognition and affirmation of different ways of life. There is something in this complaint, since nobody enjoys being put up with. Yet the modesty of toleration is also its strength. It asks citizens who disagree deeply to share a political life without first requiring them to approve of one another, which is fortunate, because in a diverse society such approval is not going to be forthcoming. A demand for universal affirmation sounds more generous, but it may ask for what people cannot sincerely give.

passage: A persistent habit of literary talk treats the short story as a smaller novel: the same materials of character, setting and incident, simply supplied in lesser quantities. On this view the story is where writers practise before attempting the larger form, and a collection of stories is a kind of portfolio of novels not yet written. The habit is reinforced by publishers, who have long regarded collections as harder to sell, and by critics who praise a story for being 'as rich as a novel', as though richness of that kind were the measure of success. Prizes and anthologies have sometimes followed suit, treating a writer's stories as preparation and the first novel as the real debut.

The comparison misunderstands where a short story does its work. A novel accumulates; it earns its effects through duration, letting the reader live alongside its people for enough days that change in them can be felt as change. A story has no such time to spend. What it has instead is selection, and selection pressed hard enough becomes a kind of meaning in itself. When a story shows a woman packing a suitcase, pausing over a single photograph and putting it back in the drawer, the eleven years of marriage that the story never describes are present precisely because they are withheld. The reader does not receive them; she supplies them, and the supplying is the experience.

This is why expanding a fine story so rarely improves it. Give the woman a history, a sister to confide in, a chapter on the courtship, and the photograph becomes one detail among many rather than the point on which everything turns. The gaps that had been doing the work are filled with information, and information, however well written, is less charged than implication. The reader who had been supplying the marriage is now simply told about it, and being told is a lesser kind of participation. The story's brevity was not a limitation it laboured under but the condition of its force.

None of this means that stories and novels never meet. Some writers have plainly used stories as sketches, and more than one long novel began as a few pages its author could not leave alone. Nor is brevity a virtue in itself; a weak story can hide behind its shortness, gesturing at depths it has not earned. The claim is narrower: that when a story succeeds on its own terms, it succeeds by a method the novel mostly cannot use, and that judging it by the novel's standards will reliably mistake its strengths for omissions.

passage: Few episodes have shaken social psychology as much as the attempts, over roughly the past decade and a half, to repeat some of its best-known experiments. Among the findings that fared worst were studies of so-called behavioural priming, which reported that subtle exposure to an idea could shift what people did shortly afterwards: that reading words associated with old age made people walk more slowly down a corridor, for instance, or that being reminded of money made them less helpful. Such results were taught in lecture halls and retold in popular books. When larger and more carefully controlled attempts to reproduce several of them found effects much smaller than those first reported, or none that could be detected, the reaction within the field was bitter, and the debate quickly took on the character of a trial.

That framing has not served anyone well. It invites the question of who was dishonest, when the more troubling lesson is that dishonesty was largely unnecessary. A literature can come to look robust through practices that most of the people using them regarded as normal: running small studies, trying several reasonable ways of analysing the data and reporting the one that worked, and publishing successes while filing failures away. Each practice, taken alone, seems a minor licence. Together they make it likely that a field will accumulate striking positive results whether or not the underlying effects are real, and that the most surprising results, which are the most likely to be false, will also be the most celebrated.

It is important to be clear about what the failed replications do and do not show. They do not show that priming in general is an illusion. That encountering one word makes a related word easier to recognise a moment later is among the most reliable findings in the study of cognition, and nothing in the recent debate casts doubt on it. Nor does a failed repetition of a single study prove that the effect it sought is exactly zero; it shows that the effect, if it exists, is smaller or less dependable than the original report implied. The questions under dispute concern a particular, ambitious claim: that brief and incidental cues reliably steer complex social behaviour.

Defenders of that claim have often replied that social behaviour is sensitive to context, so that an effect obtained with one population, in one decade, with one set of materials, need not appear when any of these is changed. There is something to this. Human beings are not inert objects, and it would be strange if the meaning of a word list were identical across cultures and generations. But the reply has a cost that its proponents do not always acknowledge. The original studies were presented as revealing general features of human minds, not as local facts about particular groups of students. If the effects are so delicate that unknown features of a setting can abolish them, then those general claims were overstated, and an appeal to hidden moderators that is made only after a failure, and never specified in advance so that it could be tested, explains everything and therefore nothing.

The reforms that the episode prompted, such as registering hypotheses and analyses before collecting data and running studies large enough to detect modest effects, have costs of their own. Research becomes slower and more expensive, and fewer dazzling results will appear. That is the right trade. A science of social behaviour that publishes fewer surprises, each of which can bear weight, is worth more than one whose surprises must all be taken on trust.

passage: A common complaint about protest is that it inconveniences people who have done nothing wrong. Commuters are delayed, shops lose trade, ambulances must find another route. The complaint has some force, but it often hides an assumption that deserves to be questioned: that legitimate protest would cause no inconvenience at all. A march that nobody notices, held where nobody has to walk around it, is hardly a protest. Part of the point of gathering in public is to make a claim that others cannot easily ignore.

This is why disruption has always been close to the centre of democratic protest rather than at its edge. Groups without money, office or access to the press have few ways of placing an issue on the public agenda, and a temporary cost imposed on the wider community is one of them. Many causes now regarded as plainly just were first brought to public notice by people who were considered a nuisance, and their critics complained, in much the same terms as are heard today, that they had chosen the wrong methods and the wrong moment.

None of this means that any disruption is acceptable. The useful distinction is between disruption that seeks a hearing and disruption that seeks to impose an outcome. The first imposes a cost in order to make others pay attention; it accepts that, once they have paid attention, they may still disagree. The second tries to make it impossible for others to act on their own decision, for instance by preventing a lawful vote from taking place or by keeping people from a service they are entitled to use. Protest of the first kind is part of the argument on which democracy runs. Protest of the second kind substitutes pressure for persuasion, and a democracy can rightly limit it.

Proportion matters as well. A blockade that delays traffic for an afternoon is different from one that prevents a hospital from receiving supplies, even if both are aimed only at securing attention. Those who protest have a responsibility to choose methods whose costs bear some relation to the importance of what they are saying, and those who govern have a responsibility not to treat every inconvenience as an emergency. Neither responsibility can be reduced to a simple rule, and particular cases will always be argued over; but the alternative to such argument is worse. A society that tolerates no disruption at all has, in effect, decided that only those who already have a hearing deserve one.

passage: A familiar answer to the question of why citizens owe obedience to their state is that they have agreed to it. Few of us, of course, ever signed anything, so the agreement is said to be tacit: by continuing to live within a country's borders, using its roads and accepting the protection of its courts, a person signals consent to its authority. The view is attractive because it seems to reconcile two things that are otherwise difficult to hold together, allowing us to say that political authority is genuinely binding while also maintaining that no one is bound against their will, since anyone who objects remains free to leave.

The trouble lies in that word 'free'. We do not normally count a choice as consent unless the person had a real alternative that could be taken at a bearable cost. Imagine a mining town with a single employer that also owns every shop, and suppose the company announces that anyone who keeps buying bread at its counters has thereby accepted all of its rules. No one would treat the purchase of bread as agreement, because the only way to refuse is to give up eating or to give up the town. Leaving a country is usually costlier still: it can mean abandoning one's language, one's family, one's work and the only place one knows well. There is, moreover, a further difficulty: almost every habitable stretch of the earth is now claimed by some state, so the emigrant does not escape political authority at all. She merely exchanges one authority for another, if another will admit her. The option on offer is not freedom from rule but the choice of a ruler.

Defenders of the view have a reasonable reply. Consent, they say, comes in degrees, and the availability of exit is not nothing. A state that lets its citizens leave, and lets them take their savings with them, really does treat them differently from one that seals its borders, and it seems right to say that the first has a stronger claim on their loyalty. This should be granted. A right of exit is a genuine good, and a state that denies it has failed one important test of legitimacy.

But to grant this is not to rescue the theory. That free exit is a condition of legitimacy does not make it the source of legitimacy, any more than an unlocked door makes a house a home. If a state's authority over those who stay can be justified, the justification must come from what the state does for and to them: whether its laws are fairly made, whether its burdens are fairly shared, whether its protection is extended to all. The language of tacit consent tends to obscure this question, since it allows a state to take credit for the mere fact that people have not fled, and to treat the absence of an escape as though it were an act of agreement.
